rationale: A wins because it keeps the central risk in view: this is a pre-launch hardware company, so the honest story is the gap between promise and proof. Its line "Helio raised $7M to \"detect wildfires within minutes\" - with zero satellites in orbit and no named customer" is exactly the kind of tension a reporter can work with. B has useful instincts, but "A State Fire Agency Agreed to Work With a Satellite Company That Has No Satellites" changes "no satellite is in orbit" into a stronger fact the update does not support. That is how a decent angle becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: "pre-launch, pre-revenue hardware company" is too confident. The update says revenue is not disclosed, not that Helio has no revenue.
"confirmed titles/dates at SpaceX and Planet Labs for both founders" assumes both founders worked at both companies. The update only says the founders are ex-SpaceX and ex-Planet Labs.

"earth-observation startups are headed next: real-time alerts, not just imagery" is a good trend frame, but it still needs outside comparables before it can be pitched as a trend instead of one funded startup.
"find-journalists" is directionally right, but the founder names, agency name, detection baseline, and fund identity should be resolved before anyone starts matching reporters.
gaps_in_B: "Engineers" is invented. The update says ex-SpaceX and ex-Planet Labs founders, not engineers.
"Company That Has No Satellites" overstates the fact. The update says no satellite is in orbit; it does not say no satellites exist.
"June timing places this at the opening of Northern Hemisphere fire season" may be a useful peg, but it is not in the supplied update and needs verification before it carries an angle.

"The prevailing assumption is that fire and public-safety agencies require demonstrated, operational capability" is an unsupported premise. It turns a thin, unnamed MOU into a procurement thesis before the facts can bear it.
